105.text:
Opinions are divided as to whether animal testing is acceptable for medical research or whether it is unethical. This essay will consider both perspectives before explaining my own opinion.

On the one hand, supporters of animal testing argue that it has contributed to many life-saving medical advances. Vaccines, insulin and surgical techniques were developed with the help of animal research, and a living body is so complex that a drug cannot be judged safe from isolated cells alone. Testing on animals first also protects human volunteers from unknown dangers. A new drug for heart disease, for example, is usually tested on animals first to check for harmful effects before any person takes it. For many serious diseases, researchers argue that no alternative is yet good enough.

On the other hand, critics argue that animals suffer in experiments, and that results do not always apply to people. Creatures that feel pain are confined and harmed for human benefit, and a drug that works safely in a mouse can fail in humans, which means that animals can be both a cause of suffering and a poor guide. Cell cultures, computer models and tiny lab-grown organs are improving, and many people argue that these should replace animal tests wherever possible. Public attitudes are also changing, as more people believe that animals have rights.

In conclusion, both views have merit. Personally, I believe that animal testing is acceptable only when no alternative exists, and only under strict rules that minimise suffering, while governments and scientists should work hard to develop and use alternatives.

Góp phần vào vaccine, insulin, kỹ thuật mổ; cơ thể sống phức tạp; thử trên động vật trước bảo vệ tình nguyện viên. Ví dụ thuốc tim mới được thử trên động vật trước khi người dùng.

306.text:
Animal testing has long been a controversial part of medical and product research, and I believe that it will change considerably over the next twenty years, becoming less common as alternatives improve, although it will probably not disappear completely.

First and foremost, new technology is providing alternatives to animal experiments. Scientists can now grow tiny organs from human cells, use computer models to predict how drugs behave in the body and test substances on chips that copy the function of organs. These methods are often cheaper and faster, and they use human cells, which may predict human reactions better than animals do. A cosmetic company that tests safety on lab-grown skin, for example, no longer needs to use rabbits. As artificial intelligence improves, such predictions will become even more reliable.

In addition, rules and public opinion are moving in the same direction. Many governments already ban animal testing for cosmetics, and research bodies follow the principle of replacing animals where possible, using fewer of them and treating them humanely. Companies know that customers increasingly dislike animal experiments, which gives them a reason to switch. However, change will have limits. A whole living body is far more complex than any model, and regulators may continue to require animal studies for the safety of new medicines until alternatives are proven. Progress will therefore be steady rather than sudden.

In conclusion, animal testing is likely to change to a large extent over the next twenty years because of better technology and stronger rules, although some use for complex medical research will probably remain.

493.text:
Some scientists still rely on experiments with animals to test new drugs, while others prefer alternatives such as cell cultures and computer models. This essay will consider both perspectives before explaining my own opinion.

On the one hand, supporters of animal testing argue that it gives results that other methods cannot yet match. A living animal has blood circulation, an immune system and organs that interact, so researchers can see how a drug is absorbed, spread and removed from the whole body, and whether it harms any organ. This is essential for safety, because a medicine that seems harmless in a dish may damage the liver or heart in a living creature. A new painkiller, for example, may look safe in cells but cause serious side effects in a whole body. Regulators in many countries still ask for animal data before trials in people.

On the other hand, supporters of alternatives point out that these methods can be faster, cheaper and more relevant to people. Human cells, lab-grown organs and computer simulations can predict human reactions better than animals, whose biology differs from ours, and they avoid animal suffering. A drug that works safely in a mouse can fail in humans, wasting years and money, whereas tests on human tissue may give more reliable answers. Alternatives also allow thousands of substances to be screened rapidly.

In conclusion, both views have merit. Overall, I believe that alternatives should be used wherever they are reliable, with animal testing kept only for cases where no other method can answer the safety question.

279.text:
Life expectancy has risen in most countries over the past century, and many people now expect to live into their eighties. This essay will discuss the main advantages and challenges before explaining whether the advantages outweigh the challenges.

On the positive side, longer lives give people more time with their families and more time to contribute. Older people pass on experience, care for grandchildren and often keep working or volunteering well beyond the traditional retirement age. A grandparent in good health, for example, can help to look after grandchildren and pass on knowledge, which supports working parents. Longer lives also reflect progress in medicine, nutrition and living conditions, and they allow people to pursue new interests, study again or start new careers later in life. Many older people today are healthy, active and valuable members of their communities.

On the negative side, ageing populations raise serious challenges. Pensions and healthcare cost more as the number of retired people grows, while there are fewer young workers to pay taxes. Illnesses such as dementia become more common, and many older people suffer from loneliness. Nevertheless, these challenges can be managed. Governments can raise the retirement age gradually, encourage saving, invest in preventive health and community care, and support older people who wish to keep working. Technology can also help older people to live independently for longer.

In conclusion, the advantages of longer life expectancy outweigh the challenges, provided that societies adapt through later retirement, better care and stronger communities.

303.text:
Obesity has become a serious health problem in many countries, and interventions to help people lose weight, from surgery and drugs to structured programmes, are increasingly common. This essay will discuss the advantages and disadvantages before explaining whether the advantages outweigh the disadvantages.

On the positive side, weight-loss interventions can greatly reduce the risk of serious disease. Losing weight lowers the risk of diabetes, heart disease and joint problems and improves mobility, while surgery, drugs and structured programmes help people who have failed with dieting alone. A patient with severe obesity who has stomach surgery, for example, may lose enough weight to control diabetes and walk without pain. Improved health also brings psychological benefits, as people often feel more confident and energetic, and healthcare costs fall over time. For some patients, these treatments are the only realistic path to a healthier life.

On the negative side, however, there are real risks and costs. Surgery carries the danger of complications and requires permanent changes to eating habits, and drugs may have side effects and be very expensive. Many people regain weight after stopping a programme, and an excessive focus on appearance can lead to unhealthy attitudes to food and even eating disorders. Nevertheless, these problems can be reduced if interventions are supervised by qualified professionals, offered to those with a genuine medical need and combined with advice on diet, exercise and mental health.

In conclusion, the advantages of weight-loss interventions outweigh the disadvantages for people at serious medical risk, provided that treatment is carefully supervised and supported over the long term.

99.text:
More people are choosing to give up meat, whether for health, environmental or ethical reasons. This essay will discuss the advantages and disadvantages of vegetarian diets before explaining whether the advantages outweigh the disadvantages.

On the positive side, a well-planned vegetarian diet is good for health and the environment. People who eat more vegetables, fruit, beans and whole grains tend to have lower risks of heart disease and some other illnesses, and producing plant foods generally uses less land, water and energy than producing meat. Vegetarian diets also reduce the number of animals raised and slaughtered for food, which appeals to many people on ethical grounds. A person who replaces red meat with lentils and vegetables several times a week, for example, can reduce both their fat intake and their carbon footprint. Many vegetarians also report that they feel lighter and more energetic.

On the negative side, there are some risks. Vegetarians must make sure that they get enough vitamin B12, iron, protein and other nutrients that are plentiful in meat, otherwise they may become tired or ill. Poorly planned diets, such as those relying on chips and cheese, can be unhealthy. Eating out or sharing meals with others can also be inconvenient, and choice may be limited in some places. Nevertheless, these problems are easily managed with knowledge, careful planning and, where necessary, supplements. Dieticians and clear labels can help people to build a balanced diet.

In conclusion, the advantages of vegetarian diets outweigh the disadvantages, provided that meals are carefully planned to include all the nutrients that the body needs.
